sales.title: Jovian (AD 363-364). AV solidus (21mm, 4.42 gm, 6h). NGC Choice MS S 5/5 - 4/5. Sirmium. D N IOVIA-NVS P F AVG, pearl-diademed, draped, and cuirassed bust of Jovian right, seen from front / SECVRITAS-REIPVBLICE, Jovian standing facing in military attire, pearl-diademed head left, grounded labarum with Christogram on banner in outstretched right hand, globe in left hand under cloak, bound captive left before, head reverted; star SIRM• in exergue. RIC VIII 110. Finest certified, this example boasts glittering surfaces and practically pristine details.  Following the death of Julian II during the Battle of Samarra AD 363, the Roman army found itself deeply split between eastern and western factions supporting rival candidates for a new emperor. The Household Guard put forth Jovian as a compromise choice and the general soldiery duly acclaimed him emperor. However, Jovian's reign would take a rough start as he would be forced to sign a peace treaty with Shahpur II after failing to cross the Tigris, giving the Sasanians most of Mesopotamia and several key border cities. Jovian would try to paint the debacle as a Roman victory, but he was met by a hostile populace. In retaliation, he ordered Antioch's library to be burned down. He would do little to stop the inevitable Christian backlash against pagans who had prospered under Julian II, revoking the Edicts of Julian, and in turn upset the still predominantly pagane empire. In early AD 364, Jovian set out for Constantinople, stopping in Dadastana for a banquet. The following morning he was found dead in his bedroom, the victim of poisonous fumes from newly painted walls by a brazier. His death, whether accidental or not, would lead to the division of the Roman empire into the East and West.
